entities.span: Every displayed claim is grounded in what the visible 500 characters actually say, or is honestly labeled as unconfirmed; the design does not assert a requirement gap the model cannot verify.
Reuses spec 0012's router and spec 0010's profile queries unchanged. No new table, no new migration, no new credential.
`scoreListings()`'s concurrent dispatch pattern is the shape feature 17 (cross vendor self check) can reuse directly for its own `ai_check` calls once it is designed.

**`/search` gains a second client component, and this one exists purely for accessibility.** `FocusRecorder` / `FocusRestorer` is forced by nothing except that a reader who tabs into the list during scoring should not be thrown to the top of the document. That is a weaker forcing function and worth naming honestly. This grows a conceded boundary rather than breaking an intact guarantee.
rejected_spans: `ApplyControl` (spec 0014) was forced by a budget cost: a no JavaScript form needs a rendered response, and that response is a re-render that spends an Adzuna call.

What makes it acceptable is that the property it spends was already spent: spec 0013's Decision carries a **No longer true** amendment saying `/search` no longer ships zero client JavaScript, and spec 0014's Consequences records that "the property is gone rather than reduced" (both read on 2026-09-06).
Anyone tempted to revert it should note that the alternative is not "no client JavaScript", it is "keyboard users lose their place", because the reveal destroys the nodes either way.

entities.span: **Focus is restored, not preserved, and the two are observably different.** There is a moment, between the reveal and the restore effect, when focus really is on the body. It is short and no reader is expected to act inside it, but a screen reader may announce the document or the list before the restored control.
rejected_spans: Preserving focus properly would mean never removing the node, which means never reordering the DOM, which is the option this spec rejected.

entities.span: **The re-rank announcement and the restored focus land in the same commit, and which one a screen reader actually speaks is not ours to decide.** Many screen reader and browser pairs prioritise the focus change and drop or truncate a simultaneous polite announcement. This spec does not sequence them; it accepts that on a render which both ranks and restores, the reader may hear only the restored control. The ranking is still discoverable, on the card they land on.
rejected_spans: Both belong to the resolved content: the `role="status"` node arrives with its text already set, and `FocusRestorer` calls `.focus()` from the same subtree's mount.
because guessing at the right delay would be tuning to one pairing
Raised by the 2026-09-06 cross check, and it is the one item here that a real screen reader has to settle rather than reasoning (see `verify.md`).

entities.span: **`document.activeElement === body` is a proxy for "the reveal orphaned this reader", not a measurement of it.** A reader who clicks blank page space, or dismisses a browser dialog, moments before the reveal has focus on the body for reasons that have nothing to do with scoring, and will be moved onto a card control they never touched. It is the one path where this mechanism reproduces the defect it exists to prevent. Accepted as narrow rather than engineered around.
rejected_spans: the alternative is tracking whether the orphaning was caused by the reveal specifically, which needs more machinery than the defect justifies

entities.span: **A reader who focuses a control before the page hydrates is not recorded.** `FocusRecorder` starts listening when its own JavaScript runs. The list first appears at roughly 1.8 seconds and the ranking at roughly 14 (measured on 2026-09-06), so the unrecorded window is the gap before hydration rather than the whole 12 seconds, and a reader in it lands on the AC-17 fallback (the results list) rather than on their exact control.
rejected_spans: Closing it fully would need an inline script running ahead of hydration, which is a bigger hammer than this defect justifies.

entities.span: **CSS `order` was rejected, and it is the option that looks cheapest.** Reordering a flex list visually leaves every card in the DOM, so focus survives with no JavaScript at all. It also leaves the DOM and reading order in Adzuna's sequence, so a screen reader reads the list unranked while the screen shows it ranked.
rejected_spans: That is a WCAG 2.2 Meaningful Sequence and Focus Order failure, and it recreates in a new place the exact defect this session just fixed: the page claiming an order it does not have. It is cheaper only if the reader is assumed to be sighted.

entities.span: Scores are never cached. Every `/search` render that has results and clears the AC-7 gate spends up to 20 `ai_scoring` calls; a repeat view (a reload, a shared link, or browser back navigation) costs budget again exactly like feature 18's own open problem, now applying to a second gated call type rather than one.
rejected_spans: the same non caching precedent `job_search` itself already accepts

entities.span: `notMentionedSkills` still requires the model to judge what a role like this one "would typically value," an inference the honest label does not remove, only flags. A wrong inference now reads as an honest, hedged guess rather than a confident false claim; it is not a fix that removes the underlying judgment call.
rejected_spans: which is the fix this spec makes

entities.span: The band ignores stated preferences by design. A listing whose salary sits well below the caller's stated minimum, or that is on site when the caller wants remote, can still land in `strong_match`,
rejected_spans: since only skill and experience alignment drive the band

entities.span: The full posting is never fetched. A skill genuinely required by a posting but never mentioned in its visible 500 characters is invisible to this feature: correctly reported as neither matched nor not mentioned, rather than wrongly reported as missing, but still unreported. This is an accepted information gap, not a closed one (see Follow-up).

Sorting only once, after all 20 resolve, means the one visible reorder waits for the slowest of the 20 calls. The honest worst case is not one hung call but a vendor side outage during the batch: every card can sit at its pending indicator for the full 30 second per call timeout (spec 0012's `tiers.ts`), then settle as 20 individual failure states with no ranking at all. The page itself is never blocked, it renders immediately in unscored order, but a reader watching the list can wait the full 30 seconds for that outcome. No aggregate, shorter than 30 second deadline is added in this spec (see Follow-up); this is accepted rather than engineered around until real usage shows it matters.

The five band names and their anchor wording are this spec's own first attempt. Feature 16's eval harness against feature 15's ground truth set is the actual mechanism to prove whether they discriminate real listings well, not this spec's own reasoning alone (AC-2).

This is the first feature that actually sends a real user's profile data to `ai_scoring` in production. Spec 0012's own provisional vendor pick and its Follow-up items (the alias pinning trigger, the eval harness ranking) apply unchanged to this feature's calls.
